title: Energy shock: why oil and gas prices have risen less than expected
gist: The February 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz removed a net ~14 mb/d of oil (14% of global supply) and 20% of global LNG, yet oil only reached USD 94/bbl (+29%) and TTF gas €49/MWh (+53%) — far below the ~105% and ~81% moves historical elasticities imply. The ECB attributes the muted pass-through to a 2.5 mb/d pre-shock oil surplus, record Chinese inventories, collapsing Asian demand and weak Asian competition for spot LNG — buffers that would erode if the Strait stays shut.

themes.theme: Hormuz shock size versus the muted oil price response

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz after US, Israeli and Iranian strikes in late February 2026 interrupted around 20 million barrels per day of transit — one-fifth of global oil supply — and even after Saudi and Emirati pipeline workarounds has caused an average realised loss of about 14 mb/d, or 14% of global supply, versus roughly 1 mb/d (1%) during the Ukraine war.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The physical oil disruption is roughly 14x the Ukraine shock; any repricing toward historical norms would be violent, so the current calm is a positioning asymmetry not a fundamentals all-clear.
insights.quote: the conflict has nevertheless resulted in an average supply loss of around 14 mb/d so far, representing 14% of global oil supply
insights.locator: The Iran war has disrupted oil supply more severely

insights.claim: Historical elasticities from Caldara et al. (2019) imply a supply disruption of the Hormuz magnitude should push oil prices up by as much as 105%, but by early June 2026 crude stood at only around USD 94 per barrel, 29% above pre-conflict levels, after retreating from a peak gain of more than 50%.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Oil is trading ~75 percentage points below its historically implied shock price — a large gap that closes fast if buffers erode, making cheap upside optionality attractive.
insights.quote: By historical standards, a disruption of this magnitude would typically push up oil prices by as much as 105% (Caldara et al. 2019).
insights.locator: The scale of the disruption is unprecedented

insights.claim: Oil prices peaked around 30% higher after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and then stabilised at lower levels by August 2022 — a broadly similar price response to 2026 despite a far smaller underlying supply shock, showing price moves are a poor proxy for physical severity.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Do not size energy exposure off headline price moves; map the physical barrels at risk against buffers instead.
insights.locator: Similarly, prices rose by around 30% at their peak

insights.claim: The 2026 oil price increase has been concentrated in short-dated contracts, pushing the futures curve into steeper backwardation than in 2022, which signals that investors are paying a premium for immediate physical availability and see elevated near-term upside risk.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Steep backwardation means positive roll yield for long crude holders and flags prompt-barrel scarcity — watch the front spread as the real-time stress gauge on Hormuz.
insights.quote: This suggests that investors placed a higher value on immediate oil availability in 2026 than they did in 2022, pointing to elevated near-term upside risks to oil prices associated with the Iran war.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the oil futures market tells a similar story

themes.theme: Why the oil market absorbed the shock: surplus, stocks, demand, policy

insights.claim: The oil market entered the Iran conflict with a supply surplus of around 2.5 mb/d — underpinned by record US shale output and China's shift to electric vehicles — versus a roughly 1 mb/d deficit before the Ukraine war, and supply shocks pass through to prices far less when balances are in surplus.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The pass-through is state-dependent: track the global balance, because the same headline barrels-lost number produces a very different price outcome once surplus flips to deficit.
insights.quote: the oil market entered the conflict with an oil supply surplus of around 2.5 mb/d
insights.locator: Oil markets were better prepared this time round

insights.claim: Chinese crude stockpiling lifted inventories from 92 days of import cover in 2023 to around 115 days by early 2026, adding a buffer on top of larger OECD stocks that cushioned the Hormuz supply loss.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: China's 23-day increase in import cover is the single largest private shock absorber in this crisis; its drawdown rate is the lead indicator for when prices break higher.
insights.quote: Chinese inventories are estimated to have risen from 92 days of import cover in 2023 to around 115 days by early 2026.
insights.locator: Second, inventories were significantly higher than in 2022

insights.claim: Weak Asian demand — driven by softer Chinese petrochemical consumption and lower Middle East jet fuel use — led the IEA to cut its Q2 2026 global oil demand forecast by 3 mb/d versus its January outlook and to project a roughly 2% year-on-year decline, a contraction far larger than the 0.6 mb/d shortfall seen in Q2 2022.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Demand destruction of 3 mb/d is doing more to offset the shock than any supply response — a bearish setup for refiners and crude if the Strait reopens.
insights.locator: Third, lower demand, particularly in Asia

insights.claim: Policymakers responded far more forcefully in 2026, with the IEA coordinating a strategic release of 400 million barrels of oil inventories against just 182 million barrels in 2022.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A 400 mb release is a one-shot buffer that must eventually be rebuilt — creating latent forward demand for crude once the crisis resolves.
insights.quote: The IEA’s coordinated strategic release of oil inventories of 400 million barrels far exceeded the 182 million barrels released in 2022.
insights.locator: Finally, policymakers have reacted more forcefully

themes.theme: Gas: same shock size, different plumbing, smaller price move

insights.claim: Both conflicts removed supply equal to about 9% of combined Asian and European gas demand, but the Iran war hit the global LNG market — the Strait of Hormuz carries 20% of global LNG supply, around 110 bcm a year — whereas the Ukraine war hit pipeline gas concentrated in Europe, with Russian exports to the region falling 126 bcm in 2022.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The 2026 gas shock is global and diffuse rather than European and concentrated, which spreads the price impact across regions instead of squeezing one benchmark.
insights.quote: The Strait of Hormuz accounts for 20% of global LNG supply, equivalent to around 110 billion cubic metres (bcm) annually
insights.locator: Similar gas disruptions, smaller price increases

insights.claim: European TTF gas prices rose 53% to €49 per megawatt-hour by early June 2026, well short of the roughly 81% increase historical elasticities imply and of the 79% rise recorded during the Ukraine war, despite a comparably sized supply shock.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: TTF is underpricing its own historical shock elasticity by ~28 percentage points; European gas call options look cheap relative to the model-implied move.
insights.locator: By early June, Title Transfer Facility (TTF) natural gas prices

insights.claim: The 2026 TTF rally is driven largely by precautionary demand shocks rather than physical shortfall because Europe's direct dependence on Middle Eastern LNG is limited, whereas in 2022 an initial precautionary move was amplified by genuine physical tightness as Russian pipeline flows collapsed.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Fear-driven rallies mean-revert when headlines fade; physical-shortage rallies do not — this one is currently the former, so fade spikes unless European molecules actually go missing.
insights.quote: price pressures increased owing to concerns over potential disruptions rather than actual supply losses, as Europe’s direct dependence on Middle Eastern LNG remains limited
insights.locator: Adolfsen et al. (2026) suggest that the recent increase

insights.claim: The gas futures curve confirms the market treats the Iran shock as transient: one and two-year TTF futures rose just 12% and 2%, against 38% and 74% over the equivalent stretch of the Ukraine conflict.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A near-flat two-year gas curve means European industrial hedging costs are low today — an attractive window to lock forward energy costs before any repricing.
insights.quote: one and two-year futures rose by 12% and 2% during the Iran war, compared with 38% and 74% during the Ukraine conflict
insights.locator: The gas futures curve also indicated a more muted price reaction

themes.theme: The LNG arbitrage: who bids for the marginal cargo

insights.claim: Europe entered 2026 with TTF between €28 and €40 per MWh thanks to diversification away from Russian gas and expanded LNG import capacity, versus €80 to €90 per MWh and heavy Russian pipeline reliance ahead of the February 2022 invasion — while storage levels were low and broadly comparable in both episodes.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The starting price level, not storage, was the key difference — Europe's regasification buildout converted a structural vulnerability into a shock absorber.
insights.locator: First, the pre-shock conditions were favourable

insights.claim: In 2022 the JKM-TTF spread turned sharply negative as Europe outbid Asia for spot cargoes while also fighting weak hydropower and nuclear output, pulling LNG westward; in March 2026 the spread turned positive, incentivising cargoes toward Asia, but its much smaller magnitude signals far less aggressive Asian buying.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The JKM-TTF spread is the cleanest real-time gauge of global gas stress — its magnitude, not its sign, tells you how violent the bidding war for cargoes is.
insights.locator: Second, competition with Asia for LNG shipments was weaker in 2026

insights.claim: Asian LNG demand fell far more sharply in 2026 than in 2022 because gas-to-coal substitution and China's more diversified energy mix give Asian buyers genuine demand flexibility, structurally capping how high global gas prices can run on a supply shock.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Asian fuel-switching capacity is now a persistent ceiling on LNG spike risk — bearish for long-dated LNG price assumptions and for greenfield export project economics.
insights.quote: reflecting greater demand flexibility thanks to gas-to-coal substitution and China’s more diversified energy mix
insights.locator: By contrast, the JKM-TTF spread turned positive in March 2026

themes.theme: Framework and two-sided risk from here

insights.claim: The central lesson from comparing the Iran and Ukraine wars is that the size of an energy supply disruption alone does not determine the price response — initial market conditions, inventories, demand flexibility and expectations can matter just as much.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Build energy shock models on a state-dependent basis: the same barrels lost produce wildly different prices depending on the buffer stack in place when the shock lands.
insights.quote: the size of an energy supply disruption alone does not determine the price response. Initial market conditions, inventories, demand flexibility and expectations can all be just as important.

insights.claim: A prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz would gradually deplete existing buffers and global inventories and force markets to abandon expectations of a rapid resolution, raising the risk of renewed upward price pressure — a risk already visible in the energy price surge triggered by the resumption of US-Iran strikes in July 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The muted price regime is conditional on a fast resolution; inventory drawdown data is the trigger to flip from short-vol to long energy exposure.
insights.quote: A prolonged closure would gradually deplete the existing buffers and global inventories while forcing markets to abandon expectations of a rapid resolution, thus increasing the risk of renewed upward price pressures.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, conditions in the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: A sustained reopening of the Strait could exert significant downward pressure on prices because oil and gas markets entered 2026 already expecting sizeable supply surpluses, and those surplus expectations may have strengthened as the conflict pushes consumers to switch faster toward alternative, more reliable energy sources.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The downside case is larger than usual: a de-escalation would release a supply surplus into a market with structurally accelerated demand substitution — bearish for hydrocarbon producers, supportive for transition assets.
